samples: This program prints a small plain-text statement for two hard-coded sample invoices (ACME and Globex), sorted by customer name. Each row shows the customer, the number of lines and the invoice total in fixed-width columns, followed by a grand total, which comes to 30.00 (9.00 for ACME after its 10% discount, plus 21.00 for Globex). It reuses an invoice module for the totals, with the discount applied and the result rounded to cents, but it reads no input and only writes to the console, so it is a demo or template you would adapt rather than a ready-made reporting tool.

This program prints a fixed-width text statement with one row per invoice, showing the customer name, the number of lines and the discounted total rounded to cents. The rows are sorted by customer, and a grand total follows. It uses only two hardcoded sample invoices (ACME and Globex) and takes no input, so it is a demonstration rather than a ready-to-use report tool. The totals come from the separate invoice module, and the only capability the program needs is console output.

This program prints a plain-text statement for two built-in sample invoices (ACME and Globex), one row per customer in alphabetical order, showing the customer name, the number of lines and the invoice total in fixed-width columns. It then prints a grand total of all invoice totals, which works out to 30.00 for the samples. Each invoice total is the sum of quantity times unit price, minus a percentage discount, rounded to cents, and it is computed by the separate `invoice` module. The data is hard-coded, so this is a demonstration of that module, and the only thing it needs from the outside world is the console.

This program prints a fixed-column plain-text statement with one row per invoice, giving the customer name, the number of lines and the discounted total. It also prints a grand total at the end. It reuses an `invoice` module that computes each total from quantity times unit price, minus a percentage discount, rounded to cents. As written it is a demo, not a general tool: `main` uses two hardcoded sample invoices (ACME, 9.00 after a 10% discount, and Globex, 21.00), sorts them by customer and ends with a grand total of 30.00. It reads no input, so you would reuse its public row-formatting and grand-total functions with your own invoices rather than run it as is.

This program is a demo: it builds two hard-coded sample invoices (one for ACME with a 10% discount, one for Globex with two lines and no discount) and prints one fixed-width row per customer, sorted by name, showing the number of lines and the invoice total. It then prints a grand total of all invoice totals, which should come to 30.00 (9.00 for ACME plus 21.00 for Globex). All the money arithmetic is delegated to the `invoice` module, which rounds each total to cents, and the report only uses the console, so it is safe to run. Because the data is built into `main`, you would need to replace the sample invoices to use it for real reporting, though the row-formatting and grand-total functions can be reused as they are.
